# What's under the hood

An explanatory piece for readers who know front-end frameworks and have read
Declare's homepage, the "Why" essay and the FAQ. Declare reads like a thin DSL
over the browser; this page shows what actually compiles, what runs where,
which code handles which job, and how one program runs unchanged in the DOM,
on a single canvas, and as a native Mac window.

The page is itself a Declare program, and its figures are live views rather
than pictures: morphs are sprung scalars, and the hit-testing figure reports
the runtime's own answers. Open it with `?render=canvas` and it is the same
page, painted into one element.

Sizes quoted here were measured 2026-09-18 from real `declarec` production
builds (gzip, default level).

include [ "../homepage/fonts.declare", "parts/kit.declare", "parts/hero.declare", "parts/compile.declare", "parts/ships.declare", "parts/click.declare", "parts/hit.declare", "parts/paint.declare", "parts/hosts.declare", "parts/honest.declare" ]

// The page's palette, light and dark. A token record is the language's own
// notation for this, so the tokens are declarations rather than a JavaScript
// object a `{ }` body happens to hold — and the App spreads one over a library
// preset below, so the few library widgets on the page find every token they
// read. The five layer hues (app, lib, run, ker, host) are the page's code.

theme Paper [
    ground = #F4F6F7, panel = #FFFFFF, sunk = #EBEFF1, line = #D5DDE3,
    ink = #15202A, lead = #34434F, body = #2A3843, muted = #5B6B78, faint = #8796A2,
    codeBg = #E8EDF0,
    accent = #2F6BDE, accentHover = #1F55BD,
    app = #2F6BDE, appSoft = #E3ECFC,
    lib = #0F9488, libSoft = #DDF3EF,
    run = #CF7B22, runSoft = #FBEBD8, runSoft0 = #FDF5EB,
    ker = #C23A5C, kerSoft = #F8E1E7,
    host = #6B7788, hostLine = #9AA6B3, hostSoft = #EDF0F3
    ]


theme Ink [
    ground = #0E1418, panel = #151D23, sunk = #1A242B, line = #26333D,
    ink = #E6ECF0, lead = #BBC7D0, body = #C9D3DA, muted = #8E9DA9, faint = #66757F,
    codeBg = #1E2931,
    accent = #6E9CF5, accentHover = #93B6FA,
    app = #5F8FF0, appSoft = #17263F,
    lib = #2DB7A7, libSoft = #11302D,
    run = #E59A45, runSoft = #3A2A17, runSoft0 = #221C15,
    ker = #E3637F, kerSoft = #3A1C25,
    host = #8C98A8, hostLine = #5A6775, hostSoft = #1B242B
    ]


App [ appName = "What's under the hood · Declare",

    // hosted: when a page mounts this program in an AppIsland (the homepage's
    // Architecture view), the host provides its appearance and type (read
    // here with hostProvided), and the page lengthens instead of this app scrolling
    // itself — so the host's own page scroll carries the article. Standalone,
    // the defaults hold and the app follows the system.

    hosted: boolean = { hostProvided("hosted", false) },
    face: string = { hostProvided("face", "") },
    headWeight: number = { hostProvided("headWeight", 600) },
    inDark: boolean = { hostProvided("dark", app.dark) },
    headTrack: number = { app.headWeight >= 900 ? -0.006 : app.headWeight >= 700 ? -0.014 : -0.02 },

    // this app's full height, exposed for the host to size its island to
    // (the host reads it as `island.exposed("docH", 0)`)

    exposes = ["docH"],
    docH: number = { this.page.y + this.page.height },

    scrolls = { app.hosted ? "none" : "y" },
    theme = { app.inDark ? ({ ...SanFranciscoDark, ...Ink }) : ({ ...SanFrancisco, ...Paper }) },

    // hosted, the app paints no ground: the host's own paper shows through

    fill = { app.hosted ? null : provided("theme").ground },

    // Helvetica, as on the homepage — unless a host hands down another face

    uiFace: string[] = { app.face == "avenir" ? Faces.avenir : Faces.helvetica },
    fontFamily = { app.uiFace },
    fontSize = 17,
    textColor = { provided("theme").body },

    // the two measures every edge on the page derives from

    col: number = { Math.min(680, app.width - 40) },
    wide: number = { Math.min(1060, app.width - 32) },

    // Fig. 1's two states: the reader switches between them

    heroMode: string = "looks",
    heroActual: boolean = { app.heroMode == "is" },

    // SELECTION IS PROVIDED ONCE, here, for the whole article. `selectable` is
    // a provided value, so a container opts its subtree in and each text leaf
    // reads the nearest provision — the type classes in the kit say nothing
    // about it, and a rich-text flow is selectable by its nature regardless.
    // The controls inside the figures are unaffected: every `Control` provides
    // `selectable = false` for its own label, which is the language's rule that
    // anything you activate is not copy.

    // The air above and below the article is the column's own padding. A padded
    // view has an inside: every child is placed from it, and the automatic
    // height counts the trailing inset back in, so `docH` measures the whole
    // article.

    page: View [ width = { app.col }, x = center, padding = [72, 0, 72, 0], selectable = true,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 40 ],

        // ── the masthead ──────────────────────────────────────────────

        masthead: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 18 ],
            Eyebrow [ text = "Declare · runtime architecture" ],
            Title [ fontSize = { app.width < 700 ? 40 : 54 }, text = "What’s under the hood" ],
            Dek [ text = "Declare reads like a thin language over the browser. It isn’t. This is what a program compiles to, which code runs where, and how one unmodified program runs as a web page, on a single canvas, and in a native Mac window." ]
            ],

        // ── the lede ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

        lede: Para [ html = "If you build for the web, you carry a picture of how every UI framework works. Your components produce a tree, the framework keeps that tree in step with your state, and the browser does the rest: layout, styling, hit-testing, scrolling, text, paint. Declare invites that picture. It has components and attributes, it runs in a browser tab, and in its default mode it leaves behind an ordinary DOM. But most of what the picture assigns to the browser has moved. This page follows one program from source file to pixels: what the compiler makes of it, what ships, what happens on a click, who decides where things are and what was touched, and how drawing works. It ends with the same file running as a web page, on a single canvas, and as a native Mac app with no browser in it. Figure 1 is the short version. Switch it from <i>What it looks like</i> to <i>What it is</i>, and watch eight jobs you would expect the browser to do move into Declare’s own runtime. Most of the figures below are live: click, drag and hover them." ],

        // ── Fig. 1 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

        fig1: Figure [
            Caption [ fig = "Fig. 1 — The stack you assume, and the one that runs",
                text = "Eight jobs a web developer expects the browser to do. In Declare each of them is decided by the runtime, on every renderer; the host is left to realize the result. The same five colors mark the same layers in every figure below." ],
            top: View [
                Segmented [ x = center, width = 300, height = 32,
                    value = { app.heroActual ? "is" : "looks" },
                    choices = { [ ({ id: "looks", label: "What it looks like" }), ({ id: "is", label: "What it is" }) ] },
                    input(v: object) { app.heroMode = "" + v }
                    ]
                ],
            Plate [ pad = 0,
                stage: HeroStage [ k = 0,
                    Spring [ attribute = k, to = { app.heroActual ? 1 : 0 }, stiffness = 60, damping = 14 ]
                    ]
                ],
            keys: View [
                legend: View [ x = center,
                    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 16 ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").app }, label = "App" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").lib }, label = "Library" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").run }, label = "Runtime" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").ker }, label = "Kernel" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").hostLine }, label = "Host" ]
                    ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 01 · Compile ─────────────────────────────────────────────

        compile: Section [ num = "01 · Compile", head = "The compiler reads your dependencies, so the runtime never has to",
            Para [ html = "In React, dependencies are discovered at run time: by re-running a component, or from a dependency array you keep by hand. Declare’s compiler reads them off the source. It parses the brackets into a tree, resolves every bare name to an explicit path through the bracket nesting, extracts each <code>{ }</code> body’s read set, and type-checks every body as TypeScript against the real API of every component. What comes out is not JavaScript that builds a UI. It is a description of one: a tree, its attributes, and a wired graph of which value reads which." ],
            Para [ html = "Follow one line through it. This is the spring target from the homepage’s bouncing-ball demo, as it appears in the compiled artifact:" ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 2 — One line, through the compiler",
                    text = "The trace is copied from the compiled program, not reconstructed. The numbers pair each read-path with the load that reads it (L0 is path 0). The stack machine runs the same six tokens the kernel runs." ],
                CompileFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "The last line is the surprise. When a body is plain arithmetic over numeric slots, as most geometry is, the compiler also emits it as bytecode for a small stack machine, and the runtime hands it to the kernel. That body never runs as JavaScript at all. In the calendar, about 600 bodies take this path; the rest run as ordinary functions, called back from inside the same settle." ],
            Detail [ label = "What else ships inside the program",
                Para [ html = "<b>The library, compiled in.</b> Library components travel as Declare, alongside your own classes, and the compiler cannot tell them apart. The calendar’s production program carries 17 library classes; <code>SimpleLayout</code> arrives as its one method, <code>place()</code>. There is no component API underneath them to ship separately." ],
                Para [ html = "<b>The compiler itself, in development only.</b> While you work, the compiler runs in the page, in a worker: 4.4 MB, three quarters of it the TypeScript compiler, which serves as both the expression parser and the type-checker. That is what lets any page here edit and re-run itself. A production build runs the compiler ahead of time and ships none of it." ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 02 · Ship ────────────────────────────────────────────────

        ships: Section [ num = "02 · Ship", head = "Your program is the small part",
            Para [ html = "A production build is one file: the runtime, the kernel, and your program as data, in a single script. Here is what that file weighs, drawn to scale. Each block’s area is its share of the gzipped bundle, and the bands keep Fig. 1’s order." ],
            f3: Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 3 — A production build, drawn to scale",
                    text = { (parent.sf.build == "hello" ? "Hello world" : parent.sf.build == "calDom" ? "The calendar, DOM build" : "The calendar, canvas build") + ": " + parent.sf.shown.toFixed(1) + " KB gzipped, on the wire. Measured from real declarec builds; hover a block for what is in it. Switch builds and watch what moves: the canvas build trades the DOM backend for its own compositor and brings its own scroll physics, and a larger app mostly grows its own block." } ],
                sf: ShipsFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Three things stand out. The runtime is a floor, not a tax per feature: about 70 KB whether you ship a hello world or the calendar, because what it does (the graph, the tree, input, text) is used by every program. The <b>layout pass is 1.8 KB</b>, because the layouts themselves are Declare classes in the library, compiled into your program like anything else. And the renderer is a single block you can swap. The DOM and canvas builds differ by one backend and about 9 KB." ],
            Detail [ label = "Sizes elsewhere: development, and the Mac",
                Para [ html = "<b>In development</b> nothing is precompiled. The boot bundle carries the whole runtime with both backends, the checker and the inspector (186 KB gzipped), and the compiler loads in a worker (1.2 MB gzipped, three quarters of it TypeScript)." ],
                Para [ html = "<b>On the Mac</b>, JavaScriptCore comes with the operating system, so nothing ships to run JavaScript. The host is a 1.6 MB Swift executable. Its largest parts are the layer tree and compositing (about a third), then window chrome and native controls, then the JavaScriptCore bridge. The C kernel is 36 KB of it, linked in directly rather than loaded as WebAssembly." ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 03 · Run ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

        run: Section [ num = "03 · Run", head = "One click, end to end",
            Para [ html = "There is no render function, so there is nothing to call again. A change travels through a graph the compiler already wired, in one indivisible step the language calls the <b>settle</b>: every write a handler makes lands together, every value that read one is recomputed once, in dependency order, and nothing paints until it has all finished." ],
            Para [ html = "Here is a real one. The meter on the left is live: click it, and the swimlane replays what your click set in motion, slowed down about a thousandfold. In real time the whole trip takes about a millisecond." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 4 — What a click sets in motion",
                    text = "Lanes use the layer code. Steps 5 and 6 are the split the compiler arranged in advance: arithmetic runs in the kernel, and anything else runs as your compiled TypeScript, called back from inside the same settle." ],
                ClickFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Two things in that sequence belong to no framework you have used. Steps 2 and 3, deciding what was hit and whether it was a click, are the runtime’s, not the browser’s. That is why hover, press, click-versus-drag and gesture ownership behave identically on every renderer. And step 5 runs no JavaScript at all: the kernel owns the graph’s bookkeeping (the tables, the edges, the ordering) and evaluates the arithmetic itself, so a frame that only moves geometry, like most animation frames, can finish without entering JavaScript." ],
            Detail [ label = "Where the kernel came from, and what it replaced",
                Para [ html = "The kernel is one C file, about 940 lines, built two ways from the same source: WebAssembly for the browser (17 KB raw, inlined into the bundle) and a static library linked into the Mac host, called through JavaScriptCore’s C API. It replaced the parts of the JavaScript runtime that profiling showed were bookkeeping, not semantics: the tracking around each constraint, the per-frame geometry arithmetic, the settle’s ordering. Measured on the desktop demo, one settle dropped by more than 80%, in Chrome and on the Mac alike." ],
                Para [ html = "Nothing in the language changed to allow it. The compiler already knew every element’s attribute set, every constraint’s read set and every type; the kernel is that knowledge held in tables instead of JavaScript objects." ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 04 · Geometry and hit-testing ────────────────────────────

        geometry: Section [ num = "04 · Place and hit", head = "Where things are, and what you touched, are the runtime’s decisions",
            Para [ html = "Open a Declare page in the DOM inspector and you will find a tree of absolutely positioned <code>div</code>s with no layout CSS on them. That is not a shortcut. It is the division of labour: every box is decided before the browser hears about it, by one of three things, none of them CSS." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 5 — Who computes a view’s box",
                    text = "Text is the one place the host contributes a number: it measures glyph widths. Wrapping, line count and the resulting height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer." ],
                WhoFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "Because the runtime placed every box, it can also answer the inverse question: what is under this point? That answer decides hover, press, whether a gesture was a click, and which view a drag lands on. The figure below doesn’t compute any of it. Each view in the scene is reporting its own <code>hovered</code> fact, which the runtime keeps true with the same walk that routes a press." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 6 — Ask the runtime what is under the pointer",
                    text = "Try the rotated card’s corners, the empty-looking glass, the badge, and the child where the pane’s clip cuts it off. The walk runs in reverse paint order and stops at the first view that has declared an interest in the pointer." ],
                HitFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "On the canvas and in the Mac host there is no DOM to ask, so this walk is the whole of hit-testing: reverse child order, clip shapes subtracted, transforms inverted, scrollers corrected. In the DOM the browser finds the element and the runtime resolves it to the nearest view that declared a handler. Either way the decision about what counts, a click or a drag, the gesture yours or the page’s, is one implementation, shared. Your program can ask it directly with <code>app.viewAt(x, y)</code>, which is how drag and drop is written." ]
            ],

        // ── 05 · Paint ───────────────────────────────────────────────

        paint: Section [ num = "05 · Paint", head = "One recording, three realizations",
            Para [ html = "Most of what a view paints is attributes: a fill, a corner radius, a stroke, a shadow, text. Each renderer realizes those its own way. For the marks attributes can’t express, such as a gauge, a sparkline or an icon, a view defines <code>draw(d)</code>. It looks like canvas code, but it never touches a canvas. It <i>records</i>." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 7 — A drawing is data until a renderer consumes it",
                    text = "The listing is derived from the same value the gauge reads, so it changes as you drag. draw() is an ordinary method called from a constraint: it re-runs when something it read changes, never per frame." ],
                PaintFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "That is why a drawing costs nothing when it sits still, and why the same library icons render on a Mac with no browser in the process. A recording is plain data, so it can be replayed into an element’s own canvas, into a shared surface, into a worker, or across a process boundary into Core Graphics. The perceptual test suite holds the DOM and canvas renderings of the same program within anti-aliasing tolerance of each other, pixel for pixel." ]
            ],

        // ── 06 · Host ────────────────────────────────────────────────

        hosts: Section [ num = "06 · Host", head = "One program, three hosts",
            Para [ html = "Everything so far happens above a single seam: an interface of 58 methods such as <code>setX</code>, <code>setFill</code>, <code>setText</code> and <code>setDrawing</code>, which the runtime calls and a backend implements. A view never learns which backend it has. That is the whole of what changes between a web page, a canvas and a native Mac window. Switch hosts below and watch what stays put." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 8 — Above the seam, nothing changes",
                    text = "The same desktop program with the same four windows open, captured in Chrome with the DOM renderer, in Chrome with ?render=canvas, and in the native Mac host. Click a screenshot to switch the diagram." ],
                HostsFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "The Mac column is the one that surprises people. The host is a Swift application with no web engine in it. It runs the runtime’s own JavaScript bundle in JavaScriptCore, on a thread of its own, links the kernel in as C, and receives one flat batch of drawing operations per settle, which it applies to a tree of Core Animation layers in a single transaction. Nothing is read back on the hot path. The host answers only two questions, how wide a run of text is and how big an image is. Hit-testing, scrolling decisions and focus stay in the runtime, so the Mac cannot disagree with the browser about where a press landed. There is only one implementation of the decision. And the whole application is small: 7.8 MB, compiler included, around a 1.6 MB executable, because the operating system already supplies JavaScriptCore, Core Animation and Core Text. The Electron apps on the machine this was written on each carry 113 to 503 MB of Electron framework before any code of their own. Electron does far more, but that is the size of shipping a browser." ],
            Para [ html = "None of this makes the DOM renderer something other than a web page. It is the default because it hands the platform everything the platform does best: real text that selects and finds, the browser’s own scroll, links that ⌘-click, native form fields, and the accessibility the platform gives those elements for free — a baseline we have not yet deepened with roles and announcements. A reader would struggle to tell a Declare page from any other. The canvas renderer is the sealed one, on purpose: for surfaces that must be uniform, capturable, or constant-size however large the interface grows." ],
            Detail [ label = "What the host is still missing",
                Para [ html = "The Mac host runs the whole corpus at full fidelity, but it is a runtime environment, not yet a way to ship software: no per-app signing, installer, updates or file dialogs, the parts Electron exists to provide. Foreign web content cannot enter it either, since a <code>DOMIsland</code> needs a browser; an <code>AppIsland</code>, which hosts another Declare program, works natively, because a tenant needs only a place to put a view tree." ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 07 · Proof ───────────────────────────────────────────────

        proof: Section [ num = "07 · Proof", head = "How it stays one program",
            Para [ html = "A claim like “the same program runs everywhere” decays unless something checks it. Three things do. A perceptual suite holds DOM and canvas renders of each program to the same pixels, within anti-aliasing tolerance. A Mac gate holds the native host to per-program baselines across a corpus of real apps. And before each release a conformance oracle puts the same behavioral questions to all three renderers and requires byte-identical answers." ],
            Figure [
                Caption [ fig = "Fig. 9 — Same question, three renderers, one answer",
                    text = "The kinds of question the oracle asks. The answers are the runtime’s, so three hosts can only agree if one decision is being made in one place, which is the architecture this page has been describing." ],
                OracleFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = "That is also why the design holds even if you never leave the DOM. A language that owns its own semantics, with no stylesheet or browser layout engine to defer to, can be checked against a second realization of itself. The canvas keeps the DOM honest. And the discipline that makes a program portable is the same one that makes it mean exactly one thing." ],
            links: View [ width = 100%,
                layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 22, lineSpacing = 10 ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?render=canvas",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHover : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Reopen this page on the canvas renderer →" ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?viewer=reader",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHover : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Read this page’s source →" ]
                ]
            ],

        colophon: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],

            // nothing here claims a width — a y-axis stack never does — so the
            // rule derives its own from the parent's content box

            Divider [ ],
            Small [ width = 100%,
                text = "This page is a Declare program; every figure on it is made of views. Sizes were measured on 18 September 2026 from declarec production builds, gzipped at the default level." ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
